axes.note: The Galaxy Ring runs multiple days per charge and is easy to sleep in; the Series 12’s ~24-hour battery means a daily charge that competes with overnight measurement.

axes.name: HRV sampling & metrics
axes.note: The Series 12 samples HRV about every 5 minutes and reports Recovery HRV plus Overall HRV against a personal baseline; the Galaxy Ring gives competent overnight optical HRV.

axes.name: Sensors & health features
axes.note: The Series 12 adds a single-lead ECG and optical hypertension notifications the ring does not have.

axes.name: Data access
axes.note: HealthKit is comparatively open and now writes native RMSSD; the Galaxy Ring has no open API and limited export, so data largely stays in Samsung Health.

axes.name: Subscription / cost
axes.note: Both are $399 one-time with no subscription (Series 12 from $399 for aluminium; titanium and ceramic cost more).

axes.name: Comfort / discreetness
axes.note: A ring disappears on the finger for around-the-clock wear; the watch is a more conventional presence and less comfortable to sleep in.

headToHeads.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs Garmin Fenix 8 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Apple Watch Series 12 (7.6 vs 7.3)
headToHeads.verdict: No overall winner — it splits by use. For the newest HRV system, the best everyday smartwatch and the lower price, the Series 12 leads. For multi-week battery that makes nightly HRV effortless, plus serious training, navigation and dive tools, the Fenix 8 leads.

bestFor.a: Choose the Series 12 if you want the best everyday smartwatch with Apple’s new Recovery HRV, ECG and hypertension notifications — at $399 with no subscription.
bestFor.b: Choose the Fenix 8 if you want one no-subscription watch for serious training, outdoor navigation and diving, with a battery measured in weeks so overnight HRV is never interrupted.

axes.name: HRV metric & sampling
axes.note: The Series 12 samples HRV ~24× more often and reports Recovery HRV against your baseline plus Overall HRV; Garmin HRV Status is a solid ~3-week overnight baseline but a single model. Edge to Apple’s newer stack.

axes.name: Battery / overnight wear
axes.note: Fenix 8: up to ~28–48 days with solar. Series 12: up to ~24 hours, so the daily charge competes with overnight wear. The Fenix is almost never off your wrist.

axes.name: Sensor & health features
axes.note: Both have ECG; the Fenix 8 adds skin temperature and Pulse Ox, the Series 12 adds optical hypertension notifications. Apple’s Health Sensing System is the stronger heart-health stack.

axes.name: Training & outdoor depth
axes.note: Multi-band GPS, maps, a 40 m dive computer, a flashlight and deep training features — the Fenix 8 is in a different class outdoors.

axes.name: Everyday smartwatch & app
axes.note: Apps, payments and a clean Apple Health UI with HRV surfaced in the Heart Rate app; Garmin Connect is deep but cluttered and dated.

axes.name: Comfort for sleep
axes.note: The Fenix 8 is a large, heavy 47–51 mm watch — a lot to sleep in. The Series 12 is the easier watch to wear overnight, though it needs charging around sleep.

axes.name: Price / subscription
axes.note: Series 12 from $399; Fenix 8 from $999.99 ($1,099.99 for 51 mm Solar). Both one-time, no subscription.

headToHeads.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs Fitbit Charge 6 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Apple Watch Series 12 (7.6 vs 6.8)
headToHeads.verdict: No overall winner — two different tiers. For the deeper HRV system, ECG, hypertension notifications and a full smartwatch, the Series 12 leads. For the cheapest credible way to track HRV and sleep trends, with a battery that suits every-night wear, the Charge 6 leads.

bestFor.a: Choose the Series 12 if you want a do-everything smartwatch whose HRV is now usable as a personal trend — Recovery HRV against your baseline, ECG and hypertension notifications — with no subscription.
bestFor.b: Choose the Fitbit Charge 6 if you want an affordable, light band that tracks overnight HRV and sleep trends well enough, and you are not trying to train on the data.

axes.name: HRV depth
axes.note: The Series 12 samples HRV ~24× more often and reports Recovery HRV against your baseline plus Overall HRV. The Charge 6 reports a basic overnight figure — fine for trends, without the depth.

axes.name: Sleep tracking
axes.note: Fitbit sleep tracking is long-refined and reliable for sleep/wake (stage estimates are less consistent); the Series 12’s sleep tracking is improved but still behind dedicated sleep trackers.

axes.name: Battery / overnight wear
axes.note: Charge 6: a small, light band with a multi-day battery, easy to wear every night. Series 12: up to ~24 hours, so charging competes with overnight wear.

axes.name: Sensor & health features
axes.note: The Series 12’s Health Sensing System adds a single-lead ECG and optical hypertension notifications; the Charge 6 is optical PPG with SpO2 and respiratory rate.

axes.name: Smartwatch & app
axes.note: Apps, payments and a clean Apple Health UI with HRV in the Heart Rate app. The Charge 6 has GPS and a few Google apps, but its app pushes Premium persistently.

axes.name: Data access
axes.note: HealthKit now writes a native RMSSD type third-party apps can read; Fitbit data lives inside the Google ecosystem with limited export.

axes.name: Price / subscription
axes.note: Charge 6: $159, HRV trends free, some deeper insights on the $9.99/month Premium tier. Series 12: $399, no subscription. The Fitbit costs well under half.

headToHeads.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs Ultrahuman Ring Pro (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Apple Watch Series 12 (7.6 vs 7.3)
headToHeads.verdict: No overall winner — it splits by use case. For hands-off overnight HRV and sleep with almost no charging, the Ultrahuman Ring Pro leads. For one device with ECG, hypertension notifications, apps and a much more frequent HRV system (Recovery/Overall HRV; no independent validation against ECG was found as of October 2026), the Series 12 leads. Both are one-time purchases; the Ring Pro is the newer, less proven hardware.

bestFor.a: Choose the Series 12 if you want one do-everything smartwatch — ECG, hypertension notifications, apps, payments — with Recovery HRV and no subscription, and you accept a daily charge.
bestFor.b: Choose the Ultrahuman Ring Pro if overnight HRV and sleep are the point, you want a ring you charge roughly every two weeks, and you are comfortable being an early adopter of a redesigned product.

axes.name: Overnight HRV precision
axes.note: Practically equal: neither model has an independent validation of overnight HRV against ECG (as of October 2026); Ultrahuman has only company-run preprints. The Ring Pro records continuously from the finger and the Series 12 samples ~24× more often than before — design differences, not a measured accuracy gap.

axes.name: Battery / overnight wear
axes.note: Ring Pro: ~15 days, the best in the ring category. Series 12: about a day, so overnight measurement competes with the nightly charge. Not close.

axes.name: Everyday smartwatch
axes.note: Screen, apps, notifications and payments — the Series 12 is a full smartwatch; the Ring Pro is a screenless sensor that offloads everything to the phone.

axes.name: Extra health features
axes.note: The Series 12 adds a single-lead ECG and hypertension notifications the ring does not have.

axes.name: Subscription / cost
axes.note: Series 12 from $399, Ring Pro $479 — both one-time with no subscription. The watch is cheaper up front; neither has an ongoing fee.

axes.name: Track record
axes.note: The Ring Pro is new, and Ultrahuman’s previous Ring Air had widely reported battery failures. The redesign targets exactly that, but long-term reliability is not yet proven.

axes.name: Comfort for sleep
axes.note: A light ring is easier to wear 24/7 and to sleep in than a watch.

headToHeads.title: Garmin Venu 4 vs Oura Ring 5 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Practically equal by ONDA score (7.6 and 7.5)
headToHeads.verdict: No overall winner — it splits by use case. For overnight HRV and sleep in the most comfortable form, the Oura Ring 5 leads (previous Oura generations agreed well with ECG overnight; the Ring 5 itself has not been separately validated). For one device that also runs your training, shows a screen and never charges a fee, the Venu 4 leads. Neither current model has been independently validated.

bestFor.a: Choose the Garmin Venu 4 if you want one no-subscription device that handles training, everyday health and HRV competently, with the battery to wear it through the night — and you don’t need a dedicated overnight ring.
bestFor.b: Choose the Oura Ring 5 if accurate overnight HRV and sleep are the point, you want the slimmest always-on wearable, and the ~$6/month membership is acceptable.

axes.name: Overnight HRV precision
axes.note: Practically equal: neither model has an independent validation of overnight HRV against ECG (as of October 2026). Earlier Oura generations did well in one study of overnight recordings (13 people) and the older Garmin Fenix 6 was in the same study, but the Ring 5 and the Venu 4 themselves have not been validated. Finger vs wrist is a design difference, not a measured accuracy gap.

axes.name: Sleep tracking
axes.note: Practically equal on accuracy — neither has an independent validation of sleep staging (as of October 2026). Oura’s sleep staging has been validated only in maker-funded studies, and the Ring 5 has no independent check. The Venu 4 has the most advanced Garmin sleep tracking yet, with circadian-alignment metrics — neither model’s sleep staging has an independent validation.

axes.name: Battery / overnight wear
axes.note: Oura Ring 5: 6–9 days. Venu 4: multi-day. Both make nightly wear practical without a charging window around sleep.

axes.name: Training & everyday smartwatch
axes.note: Screen, workouts and Garmin’s training ecosystem make the Venu 4 a real sports and daily-driver watch. The ring has no display and is not a training tool.

axes.name: Subscription / cost
axes.note: Venu 4: $499 one-time, every feature unlocked. Oura Ring 5: $399 ($499 premium finishes) plus a ~$6/month membership for full data — cheaper up front, an ongoing cost after.

axes.name: Data access
axes.note: Garmin Connect plus a developer API is reasonably open for export and third-party tools; with Oura, full data sits behind the membership.

axes.name: Comfort for sleep
axes.note: The Ring 5 is ~40% slimmer and lighter than the Ring 4 — the most comfortable always-on ring. A watch is a bulkier thing to sleep in.

headToHeads.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs Whoop 5.0 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Apple Watch Series 12 (7.6 vs 7.3)
headToHeads.verdict: No overall winner — pick by whether you want coaching or a do-everything device. Whoop 5.0 leads for continuous overnight HRV, recovery-and-strain coaching and multi-day battery; the Series 12 wins for being a no-subscription smartwatch with ECG whose HRV is now usable as a personal trend.

bestFor.a: Choose the Series 12 if you want one no-subscription smartwatch — ECG, hypertension notifications, apps — with HRV that is now usable as a personal trend.
bestFor.b: Choose Whoop 5.0 if recovery-and-strain coaching drives how you train and you want continuous overnight HRV from a screenless band — accepting the ongoing membership.

axes.name: Continuous overnight HRV
axes.note: Whoop builds its recovery signal from HRV measured during sleep; the Series 12 samples often (24× more than before) but is a watch you may not wear every night.

axes.name: Recovery coaching
axes.note: Whoop’s Recovery + Strain model is the sharpest daily-readiness coach in consumer wearables. The Series 12 gives you the numbers (Recovery vs Overall HRV) but lighter guidance.

axes.name: Battery / overnight wear
axes.note: Whoop lasts 14+ days and charges on-body without removal; the Series 12’s ~1-day battery competes with overnight measurement.

axes.name: Subscription / cost
axes.note: Series 12 is $399 one-time, no subscription. Whoop is membership-only at $199–$359/year — cheaper first year, an ongoing cost forever.

axes.name: Everyday smartwatch
axes.note: The Series 12 has a screen, apps, notifications, payments, ECG and hypertension notifications; Whoop is a screenless recovery band.

axes.name: HRV metric comparability
axes.note: Apple Health now carries an RMSSD value, the statistic Whoop uses, so you can compare in kind — Apple hasn’t confirmed Recovery HRV is RMSSD.

axes.name: Data access
axes.note: Apple’s HealthKit (now with native RMSSD) is more open than Whoop’s largely closed ecosystem.

headToHeads.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Garmin Fenix 8 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Apple Watch Ultra 4 (7.7 vs 7.3)
headToHeads.verdict: No overall winner — it splits by life. For the newest HRV system, everyday smartwatch and iPhone ecosystem, the Ultra 4 leads; for multi-week battery, deep training and expedition tools, the Fenix 8 leads.

bestFor.a: Choose the Apple Watch Ultra 4 if you want Apple’s new HRV system (Recovery HRV), the best everyday smartwatch and iPhone integration, with a 50-hour battery and dive/satellite features.
bestFor.b: Choose the Garmin Fenix 8 if you want multi-week battery, the deepest training and navigation tools, and HRV Status inside an expedition-grade watch — and you live in the Garmin/Strava world.

axes.name: HRV metric & sampling
axes.note: The Ultra 4’s 2026 system samples HRV ~24× more often and reports Recovery HRV plus Overall HRV; Garmin HRV Status is a dependable overnight-baseline read but a single model. Edge to Apple on the newer HRV stack.

axes.name: Battery life
axes.note: Fenix 8: up to ~28–48 days with solar. Ultra 4: up to ~50 hours. Both clear a night, but the Fenix is essentially never off your wrist to charge.

axes.name: Sensor & health features
axes.note: Both carry a modern optical sensor with ECG; the Ultra 4 adds hypertension notifications, the Fenix 8 adds a 40 m dive computer. Roughly a wash, different strengths.

axes.name: Outdoor / training depth
axes.note: Multi-band GPS, full maps, structured training and load models, dive and expedition tools — the Fenix is in a different class outdoors.

axes.name: Everyday smartwatch & apps
axes.note: Apple Watch is the better daily smartwatch — apps, notifications, payments, watchOS polish and iPhone integration; Garmin’s smart features are functional, not delightful.

axes.name: Ecosystem
axes.note: Apple’s lock-in is a plus if you own an iPhone; Garmin is cross-platform and integrates with Strava/TrainingPeaks. Different, no clear winner.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Ultra 4 from $799; Fenix 8 from about $999. Both one-time, no subscription — the Ultra is the cheaper flagship.

headToHeads.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs Garmin Venu 4 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Practically equal by ONDA score (7.6 and 7.5)
headToHeads.verdict: No overall winner — it splits by priorities. For the newest HRV system, an ECG and iPhone integration, the Series 12 leads; for multi-day battery that makes overnight wear effortless and the Garmin training world, the Venu 4 leads.

bestFor.a: Choose the Series 12 if you want Apple’s new HRV system (Recovery HRV), a single-lead ECG and hypertension notifications, and the iPhone ecosystem — accepting a daily charge.
bestFor.b: Choose the Garmin Venu 4 if you want multi-day battery so overnight HRV is never interrupted, the Garmin training and recovery ecosystem, and no subscription — and you don’t need an ECG.

axes.name: HRV metric & sampling
axes.note: The Series 12 samples HRV ~24× more often and reports Recovery HRV plus Overall HRV; Garmin HRV Status is a dependable overnight-baseline model. Edge to the Series 12 on the newer stack.

axes.name: Battery / overnight wear
axes.note: The Venu 4’s multi-day battery makes wearing it every night for overnight HRV effortless; the Series 12’s ~1-day battery competes with the nightly charge.

axes.name: ECG & health extras
axes.note: The Series 12 has a single-lead ECG and hypertension notifications; the Venu 4 is optical-only with no ECG.

axes.name: Everyday smartwatch & apps
axes.note: Apple Watch has the deeper app ecosystem, payments and watchOS polish; Garmin Connect is capable but cluttered.

axes.name: Training / recovery ecosystem
axes.note: Garmin’s training load, recovery and multisport tools are deeper than the Apple Watch’s for structured athletes.

axes.name: Subscription / price
axes.note: Series 12 from $399, Venu 4 from $499 — both one-time with no subscription. Different money, no clear winner.

axes.name: Platform
axes.note: Apple Watch needs an iPhone; the Venu 4 is cross-platform. A plus or minus depending on your phone.

headToHeads.title: Levels vs Nutrisense (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Levels (8.2 vs 7.9)
headToHeads.verdict: It is a deliberate tie that depends on what you want. Levels for the deepest insight engine on your own; Nutrisense for a registered dietitian working through your data with you each week.

bestFor.a: Choose Levels if you trust app intelligence over human coaching, want the deepest food-by-food insight engine in the category, and are using CGM as a self-experiment instrument.
bestFor.b: Choose Nutrisense if accountability through a registered dietitian is what makes the programme work for you, and you would rather have a person interpret the data weekly than an app.

axes.name: Sensor and accuracy
axes.note: Both ship Dexcom G7 — same hardware, same accuracy, same 10-day wear. Indistinguishable on sensor.

axes.name: Insight depth (app)
axes.note: Levels has the deeper meal-impact engine — AUC decomposition, food-by-food ranking history, time-in-range views. Nutrisense is competent but less granular.

axes.name: Human coaching
axes.note: Nutrisense includes a registered dietitian (RD) for every subscriber with weekly written reviews and in-app messaging. Levels is app-only by default.

axes.name: Content library
axes.note: Levels has a substantial editorial library backed by its medical advisory board. Nutrisense leans on the coach for guidance instead.

axes.name: Integration
axes.note: Both integrate with Apple Health; Levels adds Oura, Nutrisense adds Cronometer and ketone meters. Comparable.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Levels: $399–$1,329/year membership (1–2 months of CGM included; extra CGM is an add-on). Nutrisense: $280–$310/month including the RD. Levels is the cheaper of the two — what you pay for at Nutrisense is the coach.

headToHeads.title: Stelo by Dexcom vs Lingo by Abbott (2026)
headToHeads.label: Practically equal by ONDA score (7.5 and 7.5)
headToHeads.verdict: Stelo wins on warm-up time and wear length at a small price premium. Lingo wins on cost flexibility — buy single 2-week sensors as needed without subscription.

bestFor.a: Choose Stelo by Dexcom if a 30-minute warm-up and 15-day wear matter more than the last $50/month — you get the same Dexcom G7 hardware as Levels and Nutrisense at a third of the cost.
bestFor.b: Choose Lingo by Abbott if cost is the deciding factor or you want to wear a CGM occasionally rather than continuously — single 2-week sensors at $54 each.

axes.name: Sensor accuracy
axes.note: Practically equal: maker accuracy figures do not count as evidence, and in an independent head-to-head study (Eichenlaub et al. 2025) the Dexcom G7 platform and FreeStyle Libre 3 were similarly accurate (MARD about 12% vs 11.6% against a lab reference).

axes.name: Sensor wear time
axes.note: Stelo: 15-day wear (longer than standard Dexcom G7). Lingo: 14 days. Tie in practice; slight Stelo edge.

axes.name: Warm-up time
axes.note: Stelo: 30 minutes. Lingo: 60 minutes. Stelo back on data faster after each sensor swap.

axes.name: Insight depth
axes.note: Stelo: meal-impact + daily time-in-range. Lingo: single "Lingo Count" spike score per meal — deliberately beginner-simple.

axes.name: Price flexibility
axes.note: Lingo: $54 per single 2-week sensor, with multi-sensor plans lowering the per-sensor cost. Stelo: $99 for two sensors (~30 days) or $89/month on subscription.

axes.name: No subscription required
axes.note: Lingo: full functionality with single sensors, no subscription. Stelo: hardware works without subscription but the monthly purchase pattern is the default flow.

axes.name: App ecosystem
axes.note: Both have clean iOS/Android apps with Apple Health integration. Limited third-party connectors compared with Levels.

headToHeads.title: Levels vs Ultrahuman M1 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Levels (8.2 vs 7.6)
headToHeads.verdict: Depends on what you want. Levels for the deepest glucose-only insight engine on the best CGM hardware. Ultrahuman M1 for glucose composed with HRV, sleep and recovery from an Ultrahuman ring.

bestFor.a: Choose Levels if CGM is the central instrument and you want the deepest meal-impact analysis on Dexcom Stelo (G7 platform).
bestFor.b: Choose Ultrahuman M1 if you already own (or plan to own) an Ultrahuman ring and want glucose data composed with HRV, sleep and recovery in one app.

axes.name: Sensor accuracy
axes.note: Practically equal: maker accuracy figures do not count as evidence, and in an independent head-to-head study (Eichenlaub et al. 2025) the Dexcom G7 platform and FreeStyle Libre 3 were similarly accurate (MARD about 12% vs 11.6% against a lab reference).

axes.name: Sensor wear time
axes.note: Levels (Dexcom Stelo): 15 days. Ultrahuman M1 (Libre 3 / Lingo): 14 days. Near-identical change cadence, slight Levels edge.

axes.name: Glucose insight depth
axes.note: Levels has the deeper meal-impact engine — AUC decomposition, food-by-food ranking history, time-in-range views. Ultrahuman is competent but glucose-specific depth is shallower.

axes.name: Cross-signal integration
axes.note: Ultrahuman M1 composes glucose with HRV, sleep and recovery from an Ultrahuman ring in one timeline — unique cross-modal view. Levels integrates with Oura via Apple Health but it is bolt-on.

axes.name: Coaching
axes.note: Both app-only by default. Neither includes a human coach without a separate tier.

axes.name: App and content
axes.note: Levels has a more substantial editorial library backed by its medical advisory board. Ultrahuman is polished but content-lighter.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Ultrahuman (US, M2 Live on Lingo): from $99/month subscription or $129 for a single 14-day sensor; ring optional. Levels: tiered memberships — $80/year app-only, $399/year Core (1 month CGM), $1,329/year Complete (2 months CGM); extra CGM is an add-on. Which is cheaper depends on how much you wear a sensor.

axes.name: Standalone usability
axes.note: Levels works fully on its own. Most of Ultrahuman M1’s differentiation depends on also owning an Ultrahuman ring.

headToHeads.title: Zoe vs Levels (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Levels (8.2 vs 7.6)
headToHeads.verdict: They are different products. Zoe for a science-backed nutrition reset combining CGM + microbiome + blood biomarkers. Levels for ongoing glucose insight on the best CGM hardware.

bestFor.a: Choose Zoe if you want personalised nutrition grounded in real science — Tim Spector’s PREDICT studies — fusing CGM, gut microbiome and blood biomarkers into a single food-ranking model.
bestFor.b: Choose Levels if you want continuous CGM as a self-experimentation instrument — the deepest meal-impact engine on Dexcom Stelo (G7 platform).

axes.name: Continuous CGM use
axes.note: Levels memberships include 1–2 months of CGM a year, with extra months as an add-on. Zoe runs CGM for two weeks only — the data feeds the initial ranking model and then ends.

axes.name: Sensor accuracy
axes.note: Levels: Dexcom Stelo, G7 platform. Zoe: an older 2-week Abbott Libre variant. No independent study compares the two sensors head-to-head, and maker accuracy figures do not count as evidence in ONDA scores, so this axis is a tie.

axes.name: Multi-biomarker view
axes.note: Zoe is the only programme combining CGM with gut-microbiome stool sampling and blood biomarker panels. Levels is glucose-only.

axes.name: Scientific lineage
axes.note: Zoe runs on the published PREDICT-1/PREDICT-2 studies from King’s College London (Tim Spector). Levels has a credible medical advisory board but no equivalent published trial series.

axes.name: Personalised food rankings
axes.note: Zoe’s personalised food scores are the centrepiece of the programme. Levels surfaces meal impact but does not rank foods against your own physiology long-term.

axes.name: Meal-impact analysis depth
axes.note: Levels has the deeper per-meal analytics — AUC decomposition, food-by-food history, time-in-range. Zoe’s glucose analysis is lighter and ends after two weeks.

axes.name: Raw glucose data export
axes.note: Levels supports raw data export on request. Zoe does not export raw glucose at all.

axes.name: Price (year 1)
axes.note: Zoe: £300 setup + £60/mo × 12 = ~$1,250/year. Levels: $399/year (Core, 1 month CGM) to $1,329/year (Complete, 2 months CGM). Comparable year-1 cost; Levels offers more CGM time.

headToHeads.title: Signos vs Levels (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Levels (8.2 vs 7.5)
headToHeads.verdict: Different jobs. Signos for weight loss with AI coaching pushing daily behaviour change. Levels for ongoing biohacker insight without a weight-loss framing.

bestFor.a: Choose Signos if weight loss is the primary reason you are wearing a CGM and you respond well to in-app AI nudges — meal-by-meal suggestions, exercise prompts, snack-stack advice.
bestFor.b: Choose Levels if you treat CGM as a general-purpose biohacker instrument — running protocols, tracking time-in-range, iterating on meal experiments without a weight-loss frame.

axes.name: Sensor accuracy
axes.note: Same Dexcom G7 platform and the same accuracy. Signos ships G7 (10-day wear); Levels now ships Stelo (15-day wear, no prescription). Near-identical on sensor.

axes.name: Programme goal
axes.note: Signos: weight loss via glucose-spike management. Levels: general biohacker insight. Different jobs.

axes.name: Coaching model
axes.note: Signos: real-time AI agent surfacing meal-by-meal nudges and exercise prompts. Levels: app-only insights, no real-time coaching.

axes.name: Insight depth
axes.note: Levels has the deeper meal-impact engine — AUC decomposition, food-by-food ranking history, time-in-range views. Signos is competent but weight-loss framed.

axes.name: Content library
axes.note: Levels has a substantial editorial library backed by its medical advisory board. Signos leans on the AI nudges instead.

axes.name: Behavioural directiveness
axes.note: Signos is the most directly behavioural programme in the category — it tells you what to do in the moment. Levels surfaces the data and trusts you to interpret it.

axes.name: Weight-loss outcome data
axes.note: Signos publishes company outcome data for weight-loss specifically. Levels does not market a weight-loss outcome at all.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Signos: $140–$160/month with continuous sensors. Levels: $399–$1,329/year membership with 1–2 months of CGM included; extra CGM is an add-on. Levels is cheaper for occasional CGM blocks; Signos is simpler for continuous wear.

headToHeads.title: Veri vs Levels (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Levels (8.2 vs 7.6)
headToHeads.verdict: Geography decides. Levels for US users who want the deepest insight engine on Dexcom Stelo. Veri for EU users who want a Levels-style experience in their region.

bestFor.a: Choose Veri if you are in an EU market — local availability, multi-language support, Garmin/Oura integration baked in. The right shape where Levels does not ship.
bestFor.b: Choose Levels if you are in the US — the deeper insight engine justifies the premium pricing for serious biohacker use.

axes.name: Geographic availability
axes.note: Veri: EU-focused with broad European market coverage. Levels: US-only. For European users this axis often decides the comparison.

axes.name: Sensor accuracy
axes.note: Practically equal: maker accuracy figures do not count as evidence, and in an independent head-to-head study (Eichenlaub et al. 2025) the Dexcom G7 platform and FreeStyle Libre 3 were similarly accurate (MARD about 12% vs 11.6% against a lab reference).

axes.name: Insight depth
axes.note: Levels has the deeper meal-impact engine — AUC decomposition, food-by-food ranking history. Veri is competent but a tier behind on analytical depth.

axes.name: App polish
axes.note: Both are polished consumer apps; Levels is more mature, Veri is cleaner in places. Roughly equal.

axes.name: Third-party integrations
axes.note: Veri integrates Garmin, Oura, MyFitnessPal natively. Levels integrates Apple Health and Oura. Veri has the broader EU-relevant integration list.

axes.name: Multi-language support
axes.note: Veri offers native multi-language EU support. Levels is English-only.

axes.name: Raw data export
axes.note: Both support raw glucose data export on request. Equivalent for self-experimenters.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Veri: €199 setup + €99–€129/month. Levels: $399–$1,329/year membership with 1–2 months of CGM included (US-only). Different markets and billing models — for most EU users Veri is the only real option.

headToHeads.title: Nutrisense vs Zoe (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Nutrisense (7.9 vs 7.6)
headToHeads.verdict: Different products. Nutrisense for ongoing CGM with a human dietitian. Zoe for a multi-biomarker personalised-nutrition reset grounded in published science.

bestFor.a: Choose Nutrisense if you want a registered dietitian working through ongoing CGM data with you weekly — accountability and human coaching on continuous Dexcom G7.
bestFor.b: Choose Zoe if you want personalised nutrition based on published science — CGM + gut microbiome + blood biomarkers fused into one food-ranking model.

axes.name: Continuous CGM
axes.note: Nutrisense: continuous Dexcom G7 for as long as you subscribe. Zoe: 2-week Libre phase only. Nutrisense wins on continuous data.

axes.name: Sensor accuracy
axes.note: Nutrisense: Dexcom G7. Zoe: an older 2-week Abbott Libre variant. No independent study compares the two sensors head-to-head, and maker accuracy figures do not count as evidence in ONDA scores, so this axis is a tie.

axes.name: Human expert involvement
axes.note: Nutrisense: registered dietitian assigned to every subscriber. Zoe: app-driven, no 1-on-1 coach by default. Nutrisense wins on human coaching.

axes.name: Multi-biomarker view
axes.note: Zoe fuses CGM with gut microbiome and blood biomarker panels — uniquely multi-modal. Nutrisense is CGM-only.

axes.name: Scientific lineage
axes.note: Zoe: PREDICT-1/PREDICT-2 studies from Tim Spector’s King’s College London group, published in Nature Medicine. Nutrisense: credible RDs, no equivalent published trial series.

axes.name: Programme structure
axes.note: Zoe: multi-biomarker setup phase + personalised food rankings. Nutrisense: ongoing CGM + weekly RD review. Different shapes; Zoe is more reset-oriented.

axes.name: Personalised food rankings
axes.note: Zoe’s food-ranking model is the centrepiece — scored against your physiology long-term. Nutrisense surfaces meal-by-meal impact via the RD but does not produce ranked food lists.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Nutrisense: $280–$310/month. Zoe: ~$370 setup + ~$75/month. Zoe is cheaper after year 1 because the CGM phase is bounded.

headToHeads.title: Apollo Neuro vs Pulsetto (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Apollo Neuro (7.1 vs 6.9)
headToHeads.verdict: A deliberate tie. Apollo Neuro for always-on gentle vagal modulation throughout the day. Pulsetto for stronger acute parasympathetic sessions in a programme-driven format.

bestFor.a: Choose Apollo Neuro if you want a vagal-modulation device you can wear all day — through work, sleep, training — with no electrodes, no setup, no titration.
bestFor.b: Choose Pulsetto if you want a stronger acute electrical tVNS effect in structured 4–20 minute programme sessions, and you are comfortable with neck-worn electrode pads.

axes.name: Stimulation mechanism
axes.note: Pulsetto: cervical electrical tVNS (direct vagal stimulation). Apollo Neuro: vibrotactile (an indirect, proposed route via touch receptors). Pulsetto’s mechanism is more direct.

axes.name: Acute effect strength
axes.note: Pulsetto delivers a noticeably stronger acute parasympathetic shift; Apollo’s effect is gentler and slower by design.

axes.name: All-day wearability
axes.note: Apollo is designed for passive daily wear (wrist, ankle, clip-on); Pulsetto is a session-only collar requiring active setup with gel/saline pads.

axes.name: Evidence base
axes.note: Apollo Neuro has peer-reviewed HRV/recovery RCTs from University of Pittsburgh; Pulsetto evidence is mostly company-sponsored. Apollo edges Pulsetto on independent research.

axes.name: Protocol variety
axes.note: Pulsetto: four guided programmes (sleep, stress, anxiety, pain). Apollo: seven modes (energy, calm, sleep, focus, recover, social, clear). Both broad.

axes.name: Setup friction
axes.note: Apollo: put it on. Pulsetto: collar plus saline/gel pads, replaced periodically.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Apollo: $448 on the official store, bundled with a 1-year SmartVibes AI membership (promotional prices vary). Pulsetto: $269 hardware, optional Pulsetto+ subscription. Pulsetto is clearly cheaper upfront.

headToHeads.title: Nurosym vs Pulsetto (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Nurosym (7.4 vs 6.9)
headToHeads.verdict: Depends on what matters most. Nurosym wins on evidence and disclosed parameters; Pulsetto wins on protocol variety, daily-use form factor and price.

bestFor.a: Choose Nurosym if peer-reviewed evidence and disclosed stimulation parameters are the deciding criteria, and you are running structured tVNS self-experiments where the literature reference matters.
bestFor.b: Choose Pulsetto if you want a polished daily-use cervical tVNS device with four guided programmes at an accessible price, and you are comfortable with a thinner independent-evidence base.

axes.name: Stimulation target
axes.note: Different vagus branches: Nurosym at the auricular branch (ear), Pulsetto at the cervical vagal trunk (neck). Both studied, neither proven for wellness use; the cervical approach is more direct, the auricular has the deeper literature.

axes.name: Independent evidence base
axes.note: Nurosym: about twenty independent peer-reviewed studies of Parasym devices (50+ according to the manufacturer, as of October 2026), mostly on earlier models; no depression trial and only uncontrolled long-COVID pilots. Pulsetto: one published pilot plus company-sponsored studies.

axes.name: Stimulation parameters
axes.note: Nurosym: trials that name it report 20–25 Hz and 200–250 µs; waveform proprietary. Pulsetto: documented in-app but less granular. Nurosym is the right pick for self-experimenters who reference the literature.

axes.name: Protocol variety
axes.note: Pulsetto: four guided programmes (sleep, stress, anxiety, pain). Nurosym: a single deliberately-spartan programme with user-titrated intensity.

axes.name: Form factor
axes.note: Pulsetto: lightweight neck collar — minimal setup. Nurosym: ear clip with cable tether to the control unit.

axes.name: Regulatory status
axes.note: Both CE-marked. Nurosym a medical device (Class IIa per the maker); Pulsetto wellness device. Neither FDA-cleared.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Pulsetto: $269 hardware. Nurosym: €700 (~$820). Pulsetto costs roughly a third of the price.

headToHeads.title: Truvaga 350 vs Pulsetto (2026)
headToHeads.label: Practically equal by ONDA score (6.9 and 6.9)
headToHeads.verdict: Depends on what you value. Truvaga 350 for clinical provenance (same hardware as FDA-cleared gammaCore). Pulsetto for protocol variety, daily-use form factor and lower price.

bestFor.a: Choose Truvaga 350 if hardware provenance matters — the same cervical tVNS platform as the FDA-cleared gammaCore prescription device, without the prescription gate.
bestFor.b: Choose Pulsetto if you want a polished daily-use neck collar with four guided programmes (sleep, stress, anxiety, pain) at the most accessible price in cervical tVNS.

axes.name: Hardware provenance
axes.note: Truvaga inherits the gammaCore platform — same 5 kHz burst waveform, same manufacturing pedigree as the FDA-cleared prescription device. Pulsetto is consumer-grade from the start.

axes.name: Stimulation parameters
axes.note: Truvaga uses electroCore’s clinical-derived parameter set. Pulsetto’s parameters are documented in-app but less clinically anchored.

axes.name: Protocol variety
axes.note: Pulsetto: four guided programmes plus a custom mode. Truvaga: fixed two-minute sessions with intensity adjustment. Pulsetto is broader.

axes.name: Session length and structure
axes.note: Pulsetto: 4–20 minute sessions across modes. Truvaga: fixed 2-minute sessions, app-guided usage patterns. Pulsetto fits varied use cases more easily.

axes.name: Form factor for daily use
axes.note: Pulsetto: lightweight collar — wear-and-go. Truvaga: handheld device pressed to the neck — active holding required for the full session.

axes.name: Setup friction
axes.note: Pulsetto: collar + saline/gel pads (periodic replacement). Truvaga: handheld + conductivity gel applied per session. Pulsetto wins on continuous-wear convenience; Truvaga on session-by-session simplicity.

axes.name: Session lifetime
axes.note: Pulsetto: unlimited sessions for the lifetime of the device. Truvaga 350: capped at 350 two-minute sessions before retirement.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Pulsetto: $269. Truvaga 350: $325 for 350 preloaded sessions (rechargeable Truvaga Plus $499). Pulsetto is about $56 cheaper and has no session cap.

headToHeads.title: Sensate vs Apollo Neuro (2026)
headToHeads.label: WINNER: Apollo Neuro
headToHeads.verdict: Apollo Neuro wins overall on evidence base, all-day wearability and use-case versatility. Sensate wins specifically as an evening wind-down ritual when paired sound is the part you actually want.

bestFor.a: Choose Sensate if you want a calming evening wind-down ritual you will actually use — sound-paired, comfortable, sit-down session-based — and pre-sleep relaxation is the primary job.
bestFor.b: Choose Apollo Neuro if you want passive vagal modulation through the entire day — work, training, sleep — with the strongest non-electrical research base in the consumer category.

axes.name: Mechanism
axes.note: Apollo: vibration on the skin via touch receptors. Sensate: infrasonic sound resonating in the chest. Both are indirect, proposed routes. Apollo’s mechanism has the broader evidence base.

axes.name: Independent evidence
axes.note: Apollo Neuro: peer-reviewed HRV/recovery RCTs from University of Pittsburgh. Sensate: one published stress/HRV pilot plus company-funded studies. Apollo wins independent research.

axes.name: Use cases covered
axes.note: Apollo: seven modes (calm, energy, sleep, focus, recover, social, clear). Sensate: focused on calm/wind-down with soundscape variety. Apollo is broader.

axes.name: All-day wearability
axes.note: Apollo: wrist/ankle/clip-on, designed for passive 24/7 wear. Sensate: chest-placed sit-down session-based, 10–30 minutes at a time.

axes.name: Session experience
axes.note: Sensate’s soundscape-paired sessions are the most pleasant experience in the vagus-modulation space. Apollo runs in the background; Sensate is the foreground ritual.

axes.name: Acute effect
axes.note: Sensate produces a clearer subjective shift per session because it is designed as a focused ritual. Apollo’s effect is cumulative and ambient by design.

axes.name: Subscription model
axes.note: Apollo: $448 incl. a 1-year SmartVibes AI membership. Sensate: $299 hardware + $79/year for full soundscape library. Apollo has more free functionality.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Sensate: $299. Apollo: $448 (incl. 1-year membership). Sensate is clearly cheaper at the entry tier.

headToHeads.title: Pulsetto vs Sensate (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Pulsetto (6.9 vs 6.2)
headToHeads.verdict: Electrical stimulation vs infrasonic resonance. Pulsetto is the more active, direct tVNS device — protocol variety, HRV tracking, Oura/Apple integration, and a lower price. Sensate is a gentle, passive, well-loved calming device whose sound-based mechanism has less direct evidence. Pick Pulsetto for active vagus stimulation and data; Sensate for a soothing, hands-off wind-down.

bestFor.a: Choose Pulsetto if you want actual electrical vagus stimulation (tVNS) with protocol variety, HRV tracking and wearable integration, at a lower one-time price.
bestFor.b: Choose Sensate if you want a gentle, passive, sound-based calming ritual and you prefer no electrical stimulation.

axes.name: Mechanism
axes.note: Pulsetto delivers electrical tVNS directly to the vagus nerve — a more direct approach. Sensate uses infrasonic resonance (low-frequency sound), which is soothing but a more indirect, less-established route to vagal effects.

axes.name: Data & tracking
axes.note: Pulsetto tracks HRV and integrates with Oura and Apple Watch. Sensate is a passive experience with little data feedback.

axes.name: Session feel
axes.note: Sensate is the more purely relaxing, hands-off ritual — you lie back and let the vibrations work. Pulsetto is a shorter, more active protocol.

axes.name: Evidence
axes.note: Both are lighter on independent clinical evidence than their marketing suggests — Pulsetto on tVNS outcomes, Sensate on its infrasonic mechanism. Neither is clearly ahead here.

axes.name: Price & subscription
axes.note: Pulsetto: $269 one-time (optional ~$8/mo Pulsetto+). Sensate: $299 one-time plus a ~$79/yr Sensate+ subscription for full content. Pulsetto is cheaper overall.

axes.name: Comfort & ease
axes.note: Sensate’s lie-down-and-relax format is effortless; Pulsetto’s neck-worn electrical device takes a little more setup, though sessions are short.

headToHeads.title: gammaCore Sapphire CV vs Nurosym (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Nurosym (7.4 vs 7.0)
headToHeads.verdict: Different roles. gammaCore for clinically-indicated headache patients with prescriber access. Nurosym for self-directed consumer tVNS users who want reported stimulation settings and the largest consumer trial record (mostly earlier Parasym models).

bestFor.a: Choose gammaCore Sapphire CV if you have a migraine or cluster-headache diagnosis and a prescriber willing to write for it — the only FDA-cleared non-invasive VNS device.
bestFor.b: Choose Nurosym if you want auricular tVNS at home, with the largest independent trial record of any consumer device (mostly earlier Parasym models), and you do not have an FDA-indication condition.

axes.name: Regulatory status
axes.note: gammaCore Sapphire CV: FDA-cleared (prescription) for migraine (prevention and acute treatment, age 12+), cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua. Nurosym: CE-marked in Europe (Class IIa per the maker), not FDA-cleared. Regulatory status is a fact, not a score — FDA status is neutral in ONDA scores.

axes.name: Stimulation target
axes.note: gammaCore: cervical vagal trunk directly (most direct possible non-invasive target). Nurosym: auricular branch (the most-studied non-invasive target).

axes.name: Trial evidence — within indication
axes.note: gammaCore: 30+ randomised trials for migraine/cluster headache, the regulatory reference. Nurosym hardware: about twenty independent device studies (50+ according to the manufacturer, as of October 2026), small and mostly on earlier Parasym models.

axes.name: Trial evidence — outside indication
axes.note: For HRV, stress, inflammation, depression — Nurosym hardware has the deeper published literature. gammaCore is studied specifically for headache.

axes.name: Consumer accessibility
axes.note: gammaCore: prescription-only in the US, gated by a clinician. Nurosym: direct-to-consumer, CE-marked.

axes.name: Protocol variety
axes.note: gammaCore: fixed 2-minute sessions, clinician-calibrated dose, no programme variety. Nurosym: single user-titrated programme with disclosed parameters.

axes.name: Cost
axes.note: gammaCore: ~$600 device + refill cards, insurance coverage uneven. Nurosym: €700 (~$820) one-time, no refills. Nurosym costs a little more upfront but wins on long-term ownership without refills.

axes.name: Disclosed parameters
axes.note: Both have known stimulation parameters. gammaCore’s 5 kHz burst is fixed; trials that name Nurosym report 20–25 Hz and 200–250 µs with user-titrated intensity, though its waveform is proprietary.

headToHeads.title: Hoolest VeRelief Prime vs Pulsetto (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Pulsetto (6.9 vs 6.3)
headToHeads.verdict: Depends on use case. Hoolest VeRelief Prime for short intense pre-sleep or post-training sessions. Pulsetto for daily-use programme-driven cervical tVNS.

bestFor.a: Choose Hoolest VeRelief Prime if you want short, intense parasympathetic priming around training and sleep — athlete-built, founder-published research, dual ear-and-neck targeting.
bestFor.b: Choose Pulsetto if you want a daily-use neck collar with four guided programmes (sleep, stress, anxiety, pain) and longer sessions that fit into ambient daily routines.

axes.name: Form factor
axes.note: Pulsetto: lightweight neck collar, wear-and-go. Hoolest VeRelief Prime: handheld, requires active holding to the stimulation site.

axes.name: Session length
axes.note: Hoolest: 3–5 minute sessions, higher peak intensity. Pulsetto: 4–20 minute sessions across modes. Pulsetto fits a wider range of use cases.

axes.name: Acute effect intensity
axes.note: Hoolest delivers higher peak intensity per minute — designed for short intense sessions. Pulsetto is gentler across longer sessions.

axes.name: Programme variety
axes.note: Pulsetto: four guided programmes (sleep, stress, anxiety, pain) plus custom mode. Hoolest: three intensity modes without distinct programmes.

axes.name: Stimulation targeting
axes.note: Hoolest VeRelief Prime targets either ear (auricular) or neck (cervical) with the same handheld. Pulsetto is cervical-only.

axes.name: Independent evidence
axes.note: Hoolest: founder-published HRV-recovery and sleep-onset research from Arizona State University spin-out. Pulsetto: company-sponsored studies plus one published pilot.

axes.name: Athletic use case fit
axes.note: Hoolest was designed around athletic recovery and pre-sleep priming. Pulsetto’s use cases are more general consumer wellness.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Hoolest VeRelief Prime: $279. Pulsetto: $269. Effectively equal at the entry tier.

headToHeads.title: Flow Neuroscience vs Apollo Neuro (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Apollo Neuro (7.1 vs 6.7)
headToHeads.verdict: Not really substitutes. Flow Neuroscience for tDCS depression treatment under a structured programme. Apollo Neuro for all-day vibrotactile vagal modulation in general wellness use.

bestFor.a: Choose Flow Neuroscience if you have major depression and a clinician open to a CE-marked tDCS option — the strongest regulatory and trial backing in take-home brain devices.
bestFor.b: Choose Apollo Neuro if you want passive vagal modulation through your day — general wellness, recovery, stress — without a clinical indication or programme commitment.

axes.name: Regulatory status
axes.note: Flow Neuroscience: CE-marked Class IIa medical device. Apollo Neuro: consumer wellness wearable, no medical-device clearance. Flow is the regulated option.

axes.name: Mechanism
axes.note: Flow: tDCS — 2 mA direct-current stimulation over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (active intervention). Apollo: vibrotactile, indirect vagal modulation via mechanoreceptors. Flow is more direct.

axes.name: Indication scope
axes.note: Flow: indicated only for major depression. Apollo: general wellness — recovery, focus, sleep, calm. Apollo is broader-use; Flow is narrower by design.

axes.name: Clinical evidence
axes.note: Flow: published RCTs in Lancet Digital Health and Brain Stimulation for tDCS in major depression. Apollo: University of Pittsburgh HRV/recovery RCTs. Both real; Flow’s trials are in a clinical population (major depression).

axes.name: Day-to-day use frequency
axes.note: Apollo: continuous daily wear. Flow: 30-minute structured sessions in an 8-week programme. Apollo runs in the background; Flow is foreground intervention.

axes.name: Wearability
axes.note: Apollo: wrist/ankle/clip-on for 24/7 wear. Flow: rigid headset for seated sessions only. Apollo wins on daily life integration.

axes.name: Programme structure
axes.note: Flow: structured 8-week behavioural-therapy programme combined with stimulation. Apollo: open-ended mode selection. Flow has the clinical scaffolding.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Apollo: $448 incl. a 1-year SmartVibes AI membership. Flow: £399 (~$499) + monthly therapy-app subscription. Apollo is cheaper with no required ongoing subscription.

headToHeads.title: Nurosym vs Vagustim (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Nurosym (7.4 vs 7.2)
headToHeads.verdict: Different philosophies, and Nurosym has the deeper evidence. Nurosym for the spartan single-programme approach with the larger published trial record. Vagustim for protocol-rich auricular tVNS with EU distribution.

bestFor.a: Choose Nurosym if you want the deepest peer-reviewed auricular tVNS evidence base and disclosed parameters — Parasym devices, mostly earlier models, were used in about twenty independent published studies (50+ according to the manufacturer, as of October 2026).
bestFor.b: Choose Vagustim if you want auricular tVNS with a wider preset library (stress, sleep, depression, anxiety, IBS), and you are in an EU market where Vagustim ships natively.

axes.name: Independent trial evidence
axes.note: Nurosym: about twenty independent peer-reviewed studies of Parasym devices (50+ according to the manufacturer, as of October 2026), mostly on earlier models. Vagustim: real trial base from Turkish and German collaborator groups but smaller in volume.

axes.name: Stimulation target
axes.note: Both target the auricular branch of the vagus nerve via tragus clip. Same anatomical target.

axes.name: Stimulation parameters
axes.note: Both have known pulse parameters. Nurosym: trials that name it report 20–25 Hz and 200–250 µs; waveform proprietary. Vagustim: parameter ranges per protocol preset.

axes.name: Protocol variety
axes.note: Vagustim: library of presets (stress, sleep, depression, anxiety, IBS). Nurosym: single user-titrated programme.

axes.name: Form factor
axes.note: Nurosym: single tragus clip. Vagustim: tragus clip plus optional secondary electrode pads for specific protocols. Nurosym is simpler.

axes.name: Regulatory status
axes.note: Both CE-marked medical devices in Europe (Nurosym’s Class IIa per the maker). Neither FDA-cleared.

axes.name: Brand recognition (outside EU)
axes.note: Nurosym has broader international brand recognition. Vagustim is primarily EU-focused.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Vagustim: €499 (~$540). Nurosym: €700 (~$820). Vagustim is meaningfully cheaper at the entry tier.

headToHeads.title: Muse S Athena vs Muse 2 (2026)
headToHeads.label: WINNER: Muse S Athena
headToHeads.verdict: Muse S Athena wins overall — it does everything Muse 2 does, adds sleep tracking and fNIRS, and is the only Muse you can wear comfortably overnight. Muse 2 wins only on price.

bestFor.a: Choose Muse S Athena if you want sleep tracking on top of meditation, the most comfortable form factor for overnight wear, and the fNIRS addition for prefrontal sensing.
bestFor.b: Choose Muse 2 if meditation feedback is the only use case you have and the roughly $225 price difference matters.

axes.name: EEG channels
axes.note: Both: four dry EEG electrodes. Identical electrical brain signal.

axes.name: Additional sensors
axes.note: Athena adds prefrontal fNIRS optodes; Muse 2 has PPG heart rate. Athena’s sensor fusion is unique in the consumer market.

axes.name: Sleep tracking
axes.note: Athena includes EEG-based sleep staging; Muse 2 has none. The Athena is the only Muse you can sleep in.

axes.name: Comfort and form factor
axes.note: Athena: soft fabric band, designed for overnight wear. Muse 2: rigid headband, comfortable for 10–20 min sit-up sessions only.

axes.name: Meditation content library
axes.note: Both share the same mature meditation library — calm, focus, breath, body-scan, mood.

axes.name: App and ecosystem
axes.note: Same app, same Apple Health/Google Fit integration; Athena gets slightly more polish in the newest features.

axes.name: Developer SDK access
axes.note: Both: raw EEG via the third-party Muse Direct app; first-party SDK is limited on both.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Muse 2: $249.99 one-time. Muse S Athena: $474.99 one-time. Muse 2 is about half the price.

headToHeads.title: Muse S Athena vs Mendi (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Muse S Athena (8.5 vs 7.0)
headToHeads.verdict: Complete and rich vs simple and easy. The Muse S Athena wins on measurement (EEG + fNIRS), sleep tracking and versatility; Mendi wins on simplicity, price and habit-formation for pure focus training. Choose Muse for the fuller, more capable device; Mendi if you just want an easy, cheaper, game-based focus trainer.

bestFor.a: Choose the Muse S Athena if you want the most complete brain-training headset — EEG plus fNIRS, sleep tracking and real-time neurofeedback in a band you can sleep in.
bestFor.b: Choose Mendi if you want the simplest, cheapest way to build a daily focus-training habit, with no subscription and no learning curve.

axes.name: Measurement
axes.note: Muse S Athena combines EEG (brain electrical activity) with fNIRS (blood flow) — the first consumer band to do both. Mendi is fNIRS only, which is less granular than EEG.

axes.name: Sleep tracking
axes.note: The Muse S Athena is a soft band you can sleep in, with EEG-based sleep tracking. Mendi is a focus trainer only — no sleep.

axes.name: Simplicity & habit
axes.note: Mendi is the easiest device to build a habit with — a single visual bar, productive from session one, no learning curve. Muse offers more, which is also more to learn.

axes.name: Subscription
axes.note: Neither forces a subscription — the Muse S Athena has no mandatory fee, and Mendi is a one-time purchase. A wash.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Mendi: $379 list (often discounted). Muse S Athena: $474.99. Mendi is cheaper for pure focus training.

axes.name: Versatility
axes.note: Muse spans meditation, focus, and sleep with richer data; Mendi does one thing (prefrontal focus training) and does it simply.

headToHeads.title: Neurosity Crown vs Emotiv Insight 2 (2026)
headToHeads.label: WINNER: Neurosity Crown
headToHeads.verdict: Neurosity Crown wins for developers and biohackers who want raw EEG access without subscription. Emotiv Insight 2 wins specifically for users running academic-style analysis where EmotivPRO’s toolchain is the deciding factor.

bestFor.a: Choose Neurosity Crown if you want raw EEG over JavaScript or Python (plus BrainFlow, LSL and OSC) with no subscription gate — the most open SDK in the consumer EEG market.
bestFor.b: Choose Emotiv Insight 2 if you need the EmotivPRO toolchain and its deep academic publication base, and the Pro subscription for raw-data access is acceptable.

axes.name: EEG channels
axes.note: Neurosity Crown: 8 dry electrodes across multiple cortical sites. Emotiv Insight 2: 5 semi-dry electrodes. Neurosity has broader cortical coverage.

axes.name: Signal quality
axes.note: Both consumer-grade dry/semi-dry systems. Neurosity has more channels; Emotiv has slightly cleaner per-channel signal at rest. Effectively tied.

axes.name: Open SDK access
axes.note: Neurosity: raw EEG via JavaScript and Python (plus BrainFlow, LSL and OSC), no subscription. Emotiv: SDK available, but raw-data access requires EmotivPRO subscription. Neurosity is the more open platform.

axes.name: Academic toolchain
axes.note: EmotivPRO is cited in hundreds of published academic studies. Neurosity has a smaller research footprint — the platform is younger.

axes.name: Live cognitive metrics
axes.note: Emotiv: live focus, stress, engagement, excitement, interest, relaxation — six dimensions. Neurosity: focus, calm and flow. Emotiv shows more live scores; all are each company’s own formulas, not validated measures.

axes.name: Built-in user experience
axes.note: Neurosity ships an adaptive focus-music streaming feature out of the box. Emotiv leans on the SDK ecosystem for user-facing apps.

axes.name: Comfort
axes.note: Emotiv Insight 2 is lighter and the five-arm crown is comfortable for longer sessions. Neurosity Crown is more substantial.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Emotiv Insight 2: $499 + Pro subscription (~$99/year) for raw data. Neurosity Crown: $1,499 no subscription. Emotiv is cheaper upfront; Neurosity cheaper over multi-year ownership if you need raw data.

headToHeads.title: Muse 2 vs FocusCalm (2026)
headToHeads.label: WINNER: Muse 2
headToHeads.verdict: Muse 2 wins overall — more channels, more mature ecosystem, broader meditation content. FocusCalm wins specifically on focus-and-calm training content at a slightly lower price.

bestFor.a: Choose Muse 2 if you want the most mature consumer EEG meditation experience — four-channel signal, decade-old ecosystem, broader content library at the entry-tier price.
bestFor.b: Choose FocusCalm if focus and calm training is the specific goal and the single-channel signal is acceptable for that narrower job — slightly cheaper with structured progression.

axes.name: EEG channels
axes.note: Muse 2: four dry EEG electrodes. FocusCalm: single forehead electrode. Muse has more cortical coverage and richer multi-band analysis.

axes.name: Additional sensors
axes.note: Muse 2: EEG + PPG heart rate + accelerometer. FocusCalm: EEG + accelerometer. Muse has the broader sensor stack.

axes.name: Content library breadth
axes.note: Muse: mature meditation library — calm, focus, breath, body-scan, mood, sleep (Athena). FocusCalm: focused on focus and calm training with a narrower programme set.

axes.name: Content programme structure
axes.note: Both have structured progression and game-like elements. Muse leans on guided meditation; FocusCalm leans on training-game format.

axes.name: Ecosystem maturity
axes.note: Muse: decade of releases, large community, third-party Muse Direct for raw data. FocusCalm: newer, narrower ecosystem.

axes.name: Subscription model
axes.note: Muse 2: no mandatory subscription, full core features with hardware. FocusCalm: optional FocusCalm Plus subscription gates premium content.

axes.name: Comfort
axes.note: FocusCalm: soft headband, comfortable for daily use. Muse 2: rigid band, comfortable for sit-up sessions only. FocusCalm wins on daily wearability.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: FocusCalm: $199. Muse 2: $249.99. FocusCalm is marginally cheaper at the entry tier.

headToHeads.title: Sens.ai vs Muse S Athena (2026)
headToHeads.label: WINNER: Muse S Athena
headToHeads.verdict: Muse S Athena wins overall on content maturity, sleep tracking, comfort and price. Sens.ai wins specifically when the multi-modal EEG + PBM + HRV stack is what you want.

bestFor.a: Choose Sens.ai if the multi-modal stack — EEG plus transcranial photobiomodulation plus HRV training — in a single programme is specifically the experience you want.
bestFor.b: Choose Muse S Athena if you want the most mature consumer brain-training experience — EEG plus fNIRS, deepest meditation content library, sleep tracking, no mandatory subscription.

axes.name: EEG channel count
axes.note: Sens.ai: 5 dry electrodes. Muse S Athena: 4 dry electrodes. Sens.ai has one extra channel.

axes.name: Additional sensor modalities
axes.note: Sens.ai: EEG + transcranial photobiomodulation (NIR LEDs) + HRV (ear-clip). Muse S Athena: EEG + prefrontal fNIRS. Sens.ai has three modalities vs Athena’s two.

axes.name: Active intervention (not just measurement)
axes.note: Sens.ai’s photobiomodulation is an active intervention — it does something to the brain, not just measures it. Muse is measurement-only.

axes.name: Sleep tracking
axes.note: Muse S Athena: EEG-based sleep staging, designed for overnight wear. Sens.ai: not designed for sleep — heavier headset, sit-down sessions only.

axes.name: Meditation content library
axes.note: Muse: mature library after a decade of iteration. Sens.ai: programme-driven sessions, narrower content.

axes.name: Comfort and form factor
axes.note: Muse S Athena: soft fabric band, overnight-wear friendly. Sens.ai: substantial headset, sit-down only.

axes.name: Subscription requirement
axes.note: Muse S Athena: no mandatory subscription; core features work without one (Smart Wakeup, the AI coach and curated programs need Muse Premium). Sens.ai: subscription required for full programme access.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Muse S Athena: $474.99 one-time. Sens.ai: $1,250 including a 60-day trial membership, then $300/year or $75/month. Muse is well under half the entry cost.

headToHeads.title: Mendi vs Muse 2 (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Muse 2 (7.8 vs 7.0)
headToHeads.verdict: Different modalities. Mendi for the simplest focus-training experience via fNIRS. Muse 2 for the mature consumer EEG meditation reference.

bestFor.a: Choose Mendi if you want the simplest possible neurofeedback experience — game-based prefrontal focus training, single sensor, no learning curve, no subscription.
bestFor.b: Choose Muse 2 if meditation is the deciding use case — four-channel EEG, mature content library, decade-old ecosystem, no mandatory subscription.

axes.name: Sensor modality
axes.note: Muse 2: four-channel EEG (electrical brain activity). Mendi: fNIRS (prefrontal blood oxygenation). Different signals; EEG is informationally richer.

axes.name: Sensor count
axes.note: Muse 2: four EEG electrodes plus PPG and accelerometer. Mendi: one fNIRS sensor. Muse covers more cortical surface.

axes.name: Use-case scope
axes.note: Muse: meditation, focus, breath, sleep (Athena). Mendi: prefrontal focus training only — narrower scope by design.

axes.name: Learning curve
axes.note: Mendi: a single game, no instruction. Muse 2: guided meditations require some practice. Mendi is easier to start.

axes.name: Content library
axes.note: Muse: mature library — calm, focus, breath, body-scan, mood. Mendi: a single game-based programme.

axes.name: Comfort
axes.note: Mendi: simple forehead band, easy on/off. Muse 2: rigid headband. Mendi wins on daily-wear convenience.

axes.name: Subscription model
axes.note: Both: no mandatory subscription. Muse 2’s AI coach, cognitive tracking, external audio and curated programs need Muse Premium.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Mendi: $379 list (often discounted). Muse 2: $249.99. Muse is cheaper.

headToHeads.title: Headspace vs Calm (2026)
headToHeads.label: Practically equal by ONDA score (7.8 and 7.7)
headToHeads.verdict: Headspace wins for users learning meditation as a skill. Calm wins for users who want sleep content and a broader ambient-wellness library alongside the meditation.

bestFor.a: Choose Headspace if you want to learn meditation as a structured skill — curriculum-led courses, consistent teaching voice, progression you can track over months.
bestFor.b: Choose Calm if sleep content matters as much as meditation, you want celebrity narrators (Matthew McConaughey, Harry Styles), and a broader wellness library.

axes.name: Teaching quality
axes.note: Headspace’s curriculum is taught by a small set of credible teachers (Andy Puddicombe et al.); the teaching voice is consistent and progressive. Calm rotates many teachers and celebrities, less unified.

axes.name: Library breadth
axes.note: Calm’s library is broader — meditations plus sleep stories, sleep music, masterclasses, soundscapes. Headspace is more focused on meditation proper.

axes.name: Sleep content
axes.note: Calm’s sleep stories and sleep soundscapes are category-leading. Headspace has sleep content but it is a smaller share of the library.

axes.name: Structured courses
axes.note: Headspace’s "Basics" and themed courses are the strongest structured-learning path in the category. Calm has courses but they are not the centre of the experience.

axes.name: Personalisation
axes.note: Both surface daily recommendations and remember progress; neither stands out.

axes.name: Free tier
axes.note: Both lock most content behind subscription with a thin free tier; neither is generous.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Headspace: ~$70/year. Calm Premium: $79.99/year after a 7-day trial, or $499.99 lifetime. Close enough to call a tie; Calm alone offers a lifetime option.

headToHeads.title: Headspace vs Waking Up (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Headspace (7.8 vs 7.4)
headToHeads.verdict: Different products. Headspace for an accessible, structured introduction to mindfulness. Waking Up for the philosophical and non-dual depth Headspace deliberately stays away from.

bestFor.a: Choose Headspace if you want a friendly, structured introduction to mindfulness — clear curriculum, gentle pacing, accessible teaching voice, focused on practical stress reduction.
bestFor.b: Choose Waking Up if you want meditation as philosophical inquiry — non-dual practice, philosophy and neuroscience lectures, and Sam Harris’ teaching voice.

axes.name: Teaching philosophy
axes.note: Headspace: friendly secular mindfulness, MBSR-style. Waking Up: rigorous non-dual practice plus philosophy and neuroscience. Different intents.

axes.name: Structured curriculum
axes.note: Headspace’s Basics course is the strongest beginner curriculum in the category. Waking Up has an introductory course but the rest of the library is non-linear.

axes.name: Teaching depth
axes.note: Waking Up goes deeper into philosophy and the nature of consciousness — non-dual practice, free will, the science of attention. Headspace stays practical.

axes.name: Library scope
axes.note: Waking Up: meditations + lectures from neuroscientists (Anil Seth, Annaka Harris), philosophers and teachers. Headspace: focused on guided meditations and sleep.

axes.name: Teaching voice consistency
axes.note: Waking Up is largely Sam Harris with curated guests — strong unified voice. Headspace has a smaller core team but more rotating teachers.

axes.name: Beginner accessibility
axes.note: Headspace’s onboarding is the gentlest in the category. Waking Up is friendly but assumes a more intellectually engaged user.

axes.name: Pricing model
axes.note: Headspace is ~$70/year; Waking Up is $129.99/year on the web ($149.99/year or $19.99/month in-app, 7-day trial). Headspace is cheaper at list price, but Waking Up offers a free scholarship to anyone who cannot afford it. Headspace has no equivalent open policy.

axes.name: Sleep content
axes.note: Headspace has a structured sleep section. Waking Up has sleep content but it is secondary to the meditation library.

headToHeads.title: Calm vs Insight Timer (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Insight Timer (8.0 vs 7.7)
headToHeads.verdict: Depends on what you want to pay for. Calm for premium polish, Sleep Stories and celebrity content. Insight Timer for the largest free meditation library and access to thousands of teachers.

bestFor.a: Choose Calm if sleep content is the main draw, you respond to celebrity narration, and the $79.99/year subscription is acceptable for the polish.
bestFor.b: Choose Insight Timer if you want the largest free meditation library on the market — thousands of teachers, a real free tier, and an optional US$60/year Member Plus layer.

axes.name: Free-tier depth
axes.note: Insight Timer: the full library of 360,000+ guided meditations, talks and music tracks is free. Calm: a thin free sample that funnels toward Premium. Insight Timer wins overwhelmingly here.

axes.name: Library size
axes.note: Insight Timer: 360,000+ tracks from thousands of teachers. Calm: a curated library, much smaller but more uniformly polished.

axes.name: Teaching quality consistency
axes.note: Calm’s curation produces consistent quality. Insight Timer’s open-teacher model varies — the best content is excellent, but the average is below Calm’s floor.

axes.name: Sleep content
axes.note: Calm’s Sleep Stories are category-leading — celebrity-narrated stories, sleep music, soundscapes. Insight Timer has plenty of sleep content, but it is not the centre.

axes.name: Celebrity / star teachers
axes.note: Calm: celebrity narrators such as Matthew McConaughey and Harry Styles. Insight Timer: well-known teachers (Tara Brach, Jack Kornfield) but not consumer-celebrity narration.

axes.name: Community features
axes.note: Insight Timer has groups, live events and an active community. Calm is content-only.

axes.name: Personalisation
axes.note: Calm: structured daily recommendations and progression. Insight Timer: search-driven, less algorithmic — strong if you know what you want.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Insight Timer: free, with optional Member Plus at US$60/year, 7-day free trial. Calm: $79.99/year after a 7-day trial (or $499.99 lifetime) for most content. Insight Timer is cheaper at every tier.

headToHeads.title: Medito vs Insight Timer (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Insight Timer (8.0 vs 7.4)
headToHeads.verdict: No single winner: Medito is the better pick if you want a fully free, private app with nothing to upgrade, while Insight Timer is the better pick if you want the largest free library and do not mind an optional paid tier.

bestFor.a: Choose Medito if you want a meditation app that is completely free forever, with no ads, no account and no upsells.
bestFor.b: Choose Insight Timer if you want the biggest possible choice of free teachers and sessions, with the option to pay for structured courses.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Medito: $0, no premium tier at all. Insight Timer: free library, Member Plus US$60 per year with a 7-day free trial.

axes.name: Library size
axes.note: Insight Timer lists 360,000 free tracks from thousands of teachers; Medito’s library covers the fundamentals but is far smaller.

axes.name: Account and privacy
axes.note: Medito needs no email or sign-up and its code is public; Insight Timer is built around a profile and community features.

axes.name: Ads and upsells
axes.note: Medito has no ads and no paywall; Insight Timer’s free library comes with prompts to upgrade to Member Plus.

axes.name: Structured courses
axes.note: Insight Timer Member Plus unlocks thousands of 10- and 30-day courses; Medito offers beginner-to-advanced courses for free.

axes.name: Curation and consistency
axes.note: Medito’s smaller library is consistent; Insight Timer’s open teacher model means quality varies and you curate yourself.

axes.name: Live events and community
axes.note: Insight Timer runs regular live events and has an active community; Medito has none of note.

headToHeads.title: Balance vs Headspace (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Headspace (7.8 vs 7.5)
headToHeads.verdict: Personalisation vs structured learning. Balance wins on an adaptive daily plan tuned to you and a genuinely generous free first year. Headspace wins on teaching you to meditate from scratch, a broader polished library and a large peer-reviewed evidence base. Beginners who want a guided path Headspace; people who want a plan that adapts to them, Balance.

bestFor.a: Choose Balance if you want a meditation plan that adapts to your goals and daily check-ins, and a generous free first year to try it.
bestFor.b: Choose Headspace if you want to actually learn to meditate through structured courses, with the strongest research backing and a polished library.

axes.name: Personalisation
axes.note: Balance’s adaptive engine is the most sophisticated in the category — it tailors daily sessions to your goals and brief check-ins. Headspace’s Ebb AI adapts too, but Balance is built around personalisation.

axes.name: Learning to meditate
axes.note: Headspace’s structured courses teach one technique at a time — the best on-ramp for genuine beginners. Balance guides you but is less of a curriculum.

axes.name: Free tier / trial
axes.note: Balance often gives new users a full year free — remarkably generous. Headspace’s free tier is barely a sample.

axes.name: Content library
axes.note: Headspace has the broader, more polished library across meditation, focus and sleep. Balance is leaner and plan-focused.

axes.name: Research & evidence
axes.note: Headspace has invested heavily in research, with dozens of peer-reviewed studies — the strongest evidence base among consumer meditation apps.

axes.name: Ease for beginners
axes.note: Both are approachable — Headspace via structure, Balance via a clean, adaptive plan. Genuinely a wash for a nervous first-timer.

headToHeads.title: Balance vs Calm (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Calm (7.7 vs 7.5)
headToHeads.verdict: Personalisation vs content and sleep. Balance wins on an adaptive daily plan and a genuinely generous free first year. Calm wins on the biggest, most polished library and the best sleep content in the category. Choose Balance for a guided plan that adapts to you; Calm for sleep, relaxation and sheer breadth.

bestFor.a: Choose Balance if you want a personalised daily meditation plan that adapts to you, and a free first year to try it.
bestFor.b: Choose Calm if you mainly want the best sleep stories and a huge, polished library of relaxation content to explore.

axes.name: Personalisation
axes.note: Balance’s adaptive engine tailors daily sessions to your goals and check-ins. Calm personalises which content it surfaces, but it doesn’t adapt the sessions themselves the way Balance does.

axes.name: Sleep content
axes.note: Calm is the category’s sleep leader — 500+ Sleep Stories and the best bedtime audio. Balance covers sleep but it isn’t the focus.

axes.name: Library breadth & polish
axes.note: Calm has the largest, most beautifully produced library. Balance is leaner and plan-focused.

axes.name: Free tier / trial
axes.note: Balance often gives new users a full year free. Calm’s free tier is thin.

axes.name: Guided daily structure
axes.note: Balance leads you through an adaptive daily plan; Calm leaves you to pick from the library, which suits explorers but offers less direction.

axes.name: Relaxation & mood
axes.note: Both are calming and well-made; for pure wind-down Calm’s production edges it, but Balance’s tailored sessions land personally. A wash for general relaxation.

headToHeads.title: Calm vs Waking Up (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Calm (7.7 vs 7.4)
headToHeads.verdict: Relaxation and breadth vs serious depth. Calm wins on sleep content, a vast polished library and ease for anyone. Waking Up wins on depth, rigour and a coherent philosophical path — but it costs more and isn’t for beginners. Choose Calm to wind down and explore; Waking Up to go deep.

bestFor.a: Choose Calm if you want the best sleep stories and a big, polished library for relaxation and easy everyday meditation.
bestFor.b: Choose Waking Up if you’re an experienced or serious meditator who wants depth, rigour and philosophy over a big content library.

axes.name: Sleep & relaxation
axes.note: Calm is the category’s sleep leader — 500+ Sleep Stories and the best bedtime audio. Waking Up isn’t built for wind-down.

axes.name: Depth & rigour
axes.note: Waking Up is the deepest, most rigorous app here — serious instruction and philosophy no other app attempts. Calm stays accessible and mainstream.

axes.name: Library breadth
axes.note: Calm has the largest, most polished library across meditation, sleep and soundscapes. Waking Up is a focused single path, not a big library.

axes.name: Best for beginners
axes.note: Calm is easy for anyone. Waking Up is explicitly not aimed at first-timers.

axes.name: For experienced meditators
axes.note: Waking Up rewards experienced practitioners who want a coherent path and deeper theory. Calm can feel shallow to them.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Calm Premium is $79.99/year after a 7-day trial ($499.99 lifetime). Waking Up is $129.99/year on the web ($149.99/year or $19.99/month in-app, 7-day trial), with a free scholarship for anyone who can’t afford it. Calm is cheaper.

headToHeads.title: Headspace vs Insight Timer (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Insight Timer (8.0 vs 7.8)
headToHeads.verdict: Different products. Headspace for structured learning under one teaching voice. Insight Timer for the largest free meditation library and access to thousands of teachers.

bestFor.a: Choose Headspace if you want to learn meditation as a structured skill — Basics course, consistent teaching voice, progression you can track over months.
bestFor.b: Choose Insight Timer if you want the largest free meditation library on the market — thousands of teachers, a real free tier, an optional paid layer for premium courses.

axes.name: Free-tier depth
axes.note: Insight Timer: most of the 360,000+ meditation library is genuinely free. Headspace: thin free sample funnelling to subscription. Insight Timer wins overwhelmingly.

axes.name: Library size
axes.note: Insight Timer: 360,000+ meditations across thousands of teachers. Headspace: curated library, much smaller.

axes.name: Structured curriculum
axes.note: Headspace’s Basics course is the strongest beginner curriculum in the category. Insight Timer has courses but the library is search-driven and non-linear.

axes.name: Teaching quality consistency
axes.note: Headspace: small core team, consistent voice. Insight Timer: open-teacher model, quality varies wildly.

axes.name: Top-tier named teachers
axes.note: Insight Timer: Tara Brach, Jack Kornfield, Sharon Salzberg and other premier teachers — all accessible at no cost. Headspace: smaller named-teacher roster.

axes.name: Community features
axes.note: Insight Timer: groups, live events, courses, a real community layer. Headspace: content-only.

axes.name: Personalisation
axes.note: Headspace: structured daily recommendations and progression. Insight Timer: search-driven, less algorithmic.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Insight Timer: genuinely free + optional Member Plus (US$60/year, 7-day free trial). Headspace: ~$70/year subscription required for most content. Insight Timer is cheaper at every tier.

headToHeads.title: Medito vs Headspace (2026)
headToHeads.label: Higher ONDA score: Headspace (7.8 vs 7.4)
headToHeads.verdict: No single winner: Medito is the best way to meditate without paying anything, while Headspace is worth about $70 a year if you want the most structured teaching and a research-backed program.

bestFor.a: Choose Medito if you want a fully free, ad-free app with no account, no upsells and open-source code.
bestFor.b: Choose Headspace if you are a beginner who wants clear, structured courses and a large library, and you are happy to subscribe.

axes.name: Price
axes.note: Medito: free, with optional donations. Headspace: subscription of about $70 a year or a monthly plan, after a 14-day free trial.

axes.name: Free content
axes.note: Medito: every meditation is free, with no trial and no locked content. Headspace: free content is little more than a sample.

axes.name: Privacy
axes.note: Medito needs no account and publishes its code. Headspace requires an account to subscribe.

axes.name: Teaching for beginners
axes.note: Headspace’s structured courses are among the clearest in the category; Medito covers the basics well but with less structure.

axes.name: Library size
axes.note: Headspace has a larger library across meditation, sleep, focus and life topics; Medito’s is smaller.

axes.name: Personalisation
